newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Bosnia to get over $1.2 bln for reconstruction.
newsitem.headline: Bosnia to get over $1.2 bln for reconstruction.

text.p: The international community pledged over $1.2 billion on Wednesday to help reconstruction in Bosnia in 1997, although donors insisted the Serb Republic entity was still disqualifying itself from assistance.

Hans van den Broek, the European commissioner for external relations with Eastern Europe, told a news conference that aid would be given only to those who abided by all aspects of the peace accords which ended the 43-month Bosnian war.

"Reconstruction assistance can only be directed towards those who fully cooperate," he said. "People indicted for war crimes exclude by their own behaviour their compatriots' ability to benefit from international assistance."
Van den Broek was speaking during a break in the Third Donor Conference on the Reconstruction of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a two-day meeting which ends in Brussels on Thursday.
He said the international community had pledged $1.22 billion in grants, aid and soft loans -- short of the $1.4 billion target but enough "to go a very long way towards meeting needs."

Almost half the pledged aid came from the European Union as a bloc or from individual EU nations. The World Bank, which with the European Commission co-sponsored the conference, was the next biggest contributor.

It was clear from the news conference, however, that the international community and the entities making up Bosnia still differ widely on using aid as an inducement for cooperation with the peace accords.
Bosnian co-prime minister Haris Silajdzic told journalists that those responsible "for the disgusting project of ethnic cleansing" would have won unless priority was given to resettling refugees.

"There is no point in bringing war criminals to a tribunal if their grand project remains uncorrected," he said. "Rebuilding is a priority ... People are tired of being abnormal and living abnormal lives."
Carlos Westendorp, the EU's special envoy to Bosnia, told an earlier news briefing that aid to the Bosnian Serbs should not be tied to the handover of suspected war criminals.

"If you apply conditionality in such a way that, for example, until (indicted former Bosnian leader Radovan) Karadzic is in the Hague no financial support is given, we are playing into the hands of those who don't care at all about their population," he said.
Van den Broek stressed that only indirect aid would be given to the Serbs, such as in their rebuilding road and telecommunication links with Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation.
The Serbs would also not be excluded from emergency and clearly-targetted humanitarian aid, he said.
Christiaan Poortman, the World Bank's country director for Bosnia-Herzegovina, said he expected the shortfall on $1.4 billion aid target could be reached if conditions were right.

The latest promised funds were in addition to more than $1.8 billion already pledged since the war ended. On Thursday delegates from over 48 countries and 30 international organisations will examine the finer details of how the aid will be used.
